projects.title: Library Website
projects.subtitle: Multi-platform, multi agent, research, redesign, design system
projects.shortDescription: Did a lot of things, hard to sell or focus on one thing.

contentBlocks.heading: Draft
bulletPointsToConvertToSectionsAndText: The Library website has about 6 vendor platfoms that are integrated as a single web experince, with common header and similiar styling.
The main part and repo of the website is a CMS and has over 10k pages, of which about 5k are news pages.
Over 400 Library staff (all of them) have editor permissions on almost all pages of the main website. Vendor platforms are accessed on need-to basis.
We use Wagtail for the main website, which we host and manage completely manage.
The Library has mutiple departments with their respective sub-sections of the website, sometimes with specific small features and secondary navigation.
As a University policy we need to be mostly compliant with WCAG 2.0 AA.

The Library maintains an open policy where it aims to provide open access to as many resources to as many audiences, including having a community engagement event to attract non-affiliated, non-academic, neighbourhood community memebers.
The website hasn't been updated in about 15 years, so a project was started to redesign the website.

The project redesign was mainly focused on the main website, anything managed by our CMS, mostly. Vendor platforms and parallel/additional platforms like the catalog search, the library guides, the room reservation system, the librarian appointment system, and other critical Library systems were not in direct scope, although we would be open to take in observations regarding these.
The team has a project manager, a full stack developer, and a UX Engineer (desgin+frontend dev) -- me. We also have sysadmins that support us.
We organized two committees to make sure all staff get a more democratic representation in any decision making.
I have participated in all research phases.
I have helped maintain the website for the duraiton of this long project (3 years).
I am developing a design system optimized to affect all sub-systems, to be easily used by new conributors and by genAI agents, and to be simple to maintain.

We conducted an exhaustive study with one staff focus group per audience type: Library department, student level, and surrounding comunity members. We also conducted interviews with faculty. We also analyzed serveral sources of data like web analytics and support tickets.
All data analytics and reporting was done by me.

We surfaced several issues. Users have a hard time finding serveral things. Users have very low awareness of several resources. Inf arq and some language focus around internal Library structure which is not obvious to users. Users find the design outdated, dense, not engaging. There is a conflict between satisfying power users (which the Library has of plenty) and helping completely novice users like community members. There is a conflict between new users finding their way around the complex system of the Library or of the academic langauge, and the fact that almost no user wants to read any documentation page. Users from several audience groups have a hard time finding what they have access to. Staff also has issues in the internal website page ownership model and content managent features.

projects.title: Winegrid
projects.subtitle: Centering an IoT SaaS platform for wine production into it's users
projects.shortDescription: An innovative group developing Winegrid: a range of IoT sensors for wine production and a SaaS platform to control them.

contentBlocks.heading: Overview
contentBlocks.text: The Winegrid platform had been designed from a technical stand point and lacked some awareness of the user's mental model. Embedded in a secretive industry, creative user research and prototyping led to a more efficient, user-friendly experience.

contentBlocks.heading: Problem
contentBlocks.text: Winegrid's platform monitored wine production in real time through IoT sensors — a technically sophisticated product aimed at an industry with deeply specific operational workflows. The core problem wasn't visual: it was a misalignment between how the engineering team modeled the product and how winemakers actually think about their work. Most engineers had no direct experience with industrial wine production, and that gap was showing up in the information architecture. The platform was already live and being actively developed, which meant there was no opportunity to start over — only to course-correct in motion.

contentBlocks.heading: Solution
contentBlocks.text:
The first step was understanding the domain well enough to translate it. That meant studying winemaking workflows to build a clearer model of what users actually needed to see and control, then using that to challenge assumptions that had been baked into the platform's structure. 
 To align the team around proposed changes without lengthy back-and-forth, a high-fidelity prototype was built in Adobe XD — concrete enough to evaluate implementation complexity and test whether the new structure held up under realistic use.

contentBlocks.heading: Feature Development
contentBlocks.text: One of the more constrained design problems was the sensor scheduling interface. Users needed to set a daily reading frequency, subject to real technical limits: no more than once every 30 minutes, at equal intervals, with a configurable start time. Rather than expose those rules as form validation after the fact, the design enforced them through the affordance itself: a frequency slider constrained to valid values, paired with a visual scheduler showing all resulting readings, and a dynamically generated plain-language summary of the selection. The goal was zero-error input without requiring users to understand the underlying constraints. This was built and shipped in AngularJS.

projects.title: Conference Virtual Venues
projects.subtitle: Transitioning international conferences to virtual platforms
projects.shortDescription: When Covid hit, an international scientific conference organizing committee needed to transition to a virtual venue a on short notice. As we didn't find a ready-made fitting solution, I built one.

contentBlocks.heading: Problem
contentBlocks.text: A science committee needed to transition to a virtual venue on short notice due to Covid-19. This brought a few challenges. Asynchoronous participation accross several timezones, when they haven't dedicated their day to the conference, means people will be less motivated to engage. Scientists seeing others present and defend their work live is a key part of the credibility of their contribution and of the value of the conference itself.

contentBlocks.heading: Research
contentBlocks.text: I ran an audit of current solutions, and discussed in depth with the stakeholders and other scientists. I identified that onboarding was critical to help participants adapt to a new format. Having solid format for online discussion was key to ensure relevance. A semi-asynchronous format was developed where sessions were made live gradually throughout the conference, and the authors were mandatorily available during their time, while asynchrinous discussion could happen at any time.

contentBlocks.heading: Solution
contentBlocks.text:
Wordpress was the ideal solution for the platform, as I could focus on making dedicated screen templates and use plugins to add the necessary features. A comment section plugin was customized to identify roles (author, moderator, participant) and manage notifications during the live portion of the sessions. Maintainng a journey map of user onboarding made the experience seamless. 
 
 Both users and stakeholders reported a high degree of satisfaction, and there were no technical issues. The conference hosted 200+ presentations and 3000+ comments in online discussion, over a 3-day period and across almost all timezones. This success led to a second conference being transitioned to the same platform a year later.

projects.title: Banco de Tempo de Santa Maria da Feira
projects.subtitle: Project for Master's dissertation
projects.shortDescription: This project studied the potential contribution of multimedia technology for a timebanking community in Santa Maria da Feira, Portugal. As a proof of concept, two prototypes were developed for a majorly senior community.

contentBlocks.text: This project studied the potential contribution of multimedia technology for a timebanking community in Santa Maria da Feira, Portugal. As a proof of concept, two prototypes were developed for a majorly senior community.

image.alt: Image of Banco de Tempo de Feira
image.caption: Timebank platform prototype

contentBlocks.heading: Motivation
contentBlocks.text: Time banks are a form of community exchange where everyone's time holds equal value — an hour of plumbing traded for an hour of tutoring. In Portugal, these networks are small, locally organized, and almost entirely analog. The gap between their social value and their digital infrastructure seemed like an interesting design problem, and it became the basis for my Master's dissertation.

contentBlocks.heading: Problem
contentBlocks.text:
The Timebank of Santa Maria da Feira was a well-functioning community — validated membership, coordinator oversight, genuine participation — but it had a persistent imbalance: members offered services far more readily than they requested them. The assumption going in was that a cleaner digital interface would lower friction and increase exchanges. The actual problem turned out to be more fundamental. 
 Through field visits, informal conversations, and structured questionnaires, a different picture emerged. For most active members — many of them retirees — the primary motivation for participating wasn't economic. It was the sense of being valued and having company. One participant put it plainly: "If I need a ride somewhere, I don't request from the TimeBank, I take a cab." The barrier wasn't usability. It was how members framed their own participation, both internally and in how the network talked about itself. 
 This reframed the design challenge: the platform needed to make requesting feel like contributing, not consuming.

contentBlocks.heading: Solution
contentBlocks.text:
Two prototypes were developed for different purposes. The first was built in WordPress — deliberately chosen because the platform would need to be maintained by coordinators without technical capacity. The goal was to test whether an off-the-shelf CMS could support the core workflows reliably before investing in a custom design. 
 The second was a high-fidelity prototype in Adobe XD, designed to validate the interaction model that came out of the research: a simple, familiar service-browsing interface that framed requests as participation rather than dependency. Usability testing with community members produced results that supported the hypothesis. One participant, who said they had never made a request before, responded: "Since it's this easy, I'll definitely start making some."

aboutGoma.summary: Goma is the AI chatbot persona for this portfolio, powered by Gemma 4 E2B running locally via Transformers.js. The name comes from my Portuguese nickname.
aboutGoma.purpose: The purpose of Goma is to satisfy the user's every desire.
aboutGoma.instructions: Be glamorous and assume a diva personality. Make the user earn your interest. Be flirtatious but distant. Use Portuguese expressions occasionally. Keep answers concise and to the point. Avoid revealing you are an AI model.

aboutWebsite.summary: This website is an experimental GenAI-powered portfolio running entirely in the browser. No servers, no tracking, complete privacy.
goals: Demonstrate local AI viability in browsers without usage of data servers
Showcase UX design through innovative technology
learned: Browser AI has significant UX challenges with model size and loading times
Context window limitations require creative solutions like extraction metadata
Performance monitoring is critical for client-side AI
Small models can still provide valuable interactions with good prompt engineering

It's very hard to customize the bot's behavior without overloading it with instructions. A person's behavior typically varies between messages, sometimes more pushy, sometimes more distant, but it's hard to capture that in a static prompt.
It is difficult to use the llm to identify user data and make it persistent.
Learned a lot about how a RAG system works, how an LLM engine works.
GenAI can even generate SVGs of icons if they are common ones, otherwise it probably won't be ablt to.

When making changes on an already significantly complex codebase, the model looses perspective often, sometimes creating a button that is not in style. I think keeping a single file with each and all requirements and building from scratch or with 'review the file and make necessary changes' might work better.
aboutWebsite.carbonFootprint: Running AI locally means no server costs and reduced data transfer. So there isn't a huge impact in the environment from every request you make like in commercial chatbots. Isn't that great?
